anchors.fact: Sloe gin is a British drink: the berries of the blackthorn bush steeped in gin and sweetened with sugar, traditionally poured around Christmas and New Year. (A1, S1; Oxford SLOE GIN pdf 1814, PRUNELLE pdf 1573)
anchors.meaning: Something plain, made at home, kept for the time people gather.

anchors.fact: Rural households in Britain have made it since the 1800s; with damson gin, it was a standard thing to do at harvest. (A2, S11; pdf 1814)
anchors.meaning: Know-how that lives in ordinary homes, not in a trade or a school.

anchors.fact: It reached the newspapers in the 1830s, was being made to sell by the end of that century, and had a brief vogue in America in the early 1900s (the Sloe Gin Fizz by 1904). (A3, S12, S14; pdf 1814, FIZZ pdf 794)
anchors.meaning: The trade's moment came and went.

anchors.fact: After that it fell out of favour and was missing from drinks menus for decades, apart from a slight mid-century rise with the Fizz. (A4, S13; pdf 1814)
anchors.meaning: Dropped by the menus, never said to be dropped at home. Menus only, not "the trade"; the Fizz is never said to end.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: that it stops with them

anchors.fact: In Britain it is still made from traditional recipes handed down through generations of rural families. (A5, S15; pdf 1814, "continues")
anchors.meaning: What they were given goes on being handed down. Told beside the menu decades, order-neutral: never "kept it alive", "saved", "outlasted". No named giver exists; none invented.

anchors.fact: Every winter, countryside pubs and fairs hold contests to settle whose recipe is best in the area. (A6, S16; pdf 1814)
anchors.meaning: Folk know-how tested in public by the people who keep it, and a little funny.

anchors.fact: One, the World Sloe Gin Championships, was hosted by the George Inn at Frant, open to home makers and distillers. (A7, S17; Ellis, *Severn Bites* 2016, secondary)
anchors.meaning: A village pub giving itself a world title. Past tense: never "still held".

anchors.fact: In the 2016 blind tasting, the three judges scored the top six home-made entries above every commercial one. (A8, S17; Ellis, quoting the press release)
anchors.meaning: Plain know-how holding its own. Told once, never "beat the experts".

anchors.fact: A maker who says she won it twice wrote in 2016 that she was trying the way fruit liqueurs are made in Croatia, leaving her jars in the sun. (A9, S18; Ellis 2016)
anchors.meaning: What's handed on gets tried and changed. The page never says that batch won.

anchors.fact: The Blackthorn is a name, not one recipe: one 1947 bar guide printed five quite different drinks under it, one of them gin, sloe gin, dry vermouth and orange bitters. (B1, S19; Oxford BLACKTHORN COCKTAIL pdf 280)
anchors.meaning: Many versions, one kept. The measures are Tomás's, never "Trader Vic's recipe".

anchors.fact: Bartenders have made it different ways for more than a hundred years: in 1922 a London barman wrote that it was an old drink made two ways. (B2, S20; pdf 280, Vermeire)
anchors.meaning: The argument over the right recipe is old. Paraphrase, never Felten's "great Blackthorn debate".

anchors.fact: The sloe-gin version was credited in 1908 to William Smith, bartender at Honolulu's Royal Hawaiian Hotel; his had both vermouths and Angostura. (B3, S21; pdf 280, Boothby)
anchors.meaning: A name on the recipe, as the guest keeps names on theirs. Ours isn't Smith's.
anchors.speaksTo: the giver kept in the room

anchors.fact: Of the shapes on record, this one keeps the dry vermouth because the sloe gin is already sweetened. (B4; pdf 280 + Tomás's balance, ours)
anchors.meaning: Kept what worked, and said why.

cocktail.closingLine: Sixty between the two gins, whatever the bottle. When you teach it, say how you split the sixty.
cocktail.glassware: small stemmed glass (about 150 ml), chilled, no ice
method: Put the glass in the freezer for 10 minutes, or fill it with ice and water while you make the drink.

Pour a little of the sloe gin and taste it on its own. Every bottle is sweetened by its maker, and a home-made one is sweetened to its maker's taste, so this sets your measures: the sweeter it is, the less sloe gin and the more plain gin, choosing the line from the rule. The two always add up to 60 ml.
Pour both gins, the dry vermouth and the bitters into a mixing glass (or any tall, sturdy glass) and fill it with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the mixing glass feels very cold.
Empty the serving glass if it's holding ice, then strain the drink into it. No ice in the glass.
Hold the lemon peel skin side down over the drink and pinch it between finger and thumb, so its oils fall onto the top. Then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Tried and True

recipe.note: a traditional sloe gin: bought, made by someone you know, or your own. Sloe gins can contain almond, and some makers crush the stones: if you avoid nuts, don't make this one
any London dry gin, about 43% or stronger
French-style dry white vermouth; keep it in the fridge once it's open
about the length of a thumb, with as little of the white pith as you can

recipe.item: *the rule:* the sloe gin and the gin always add up to 60 ml (2 oz)
recipe.note: most sloe gins: 30 ml of each. Sweeter than most: 22.5 ml sloe gin, 37.5 ml gin. Sweet as a syrup: 15 ml sloe gin, 45 ml gin

cocktail.tagline: Most of what you know, somebody told you. You still remember who.

reading.epigraph: In 1947, one bar guide printed five different Blackthorns. This glass is built on one of them.
whoYouAre: A friend starts a new job tomorrow and is sure they'll get it all wrong. You tell them what an old neighbour used to say: learn everyone's name on the first day, and the rest can wait. It's exactly right, and they write it down. Half of what you know came like that, with somebody's name on it, and you still hear their voice when you say it.

Here's the bit you don't say: you didn't hold on to all of it. Some of what you were told turned out to be wrong, and you let those bits go quietly, because saying so would feel like letting them down. What's left, you've tried for yourself. You can't always say why it works, only who told you, and when someone asks for the reason, you doubt yourself. The real fear is the day nobody asks. If it stops with you, a little of them stops too.
But each time you say "as my neighbour used to say", that neighbour is in the room again, and someone leaves with something to use tomorrow. You do a kindness to two people at once.
yours: Since the 1800s, households in rural Britain have made sloe gin: the berries of the blackthorn bush, left in sweetened gin and poured at Christmas and New Year. Along with damson gin, it was simply something you did at harvest.

By the end of that century it was being made to sell, and America had a short fling with it. Then for decades it went missing from drinks menus. In the countryside, the recipes went on being handed down through the generations, and they still are. Every winter, pubs and fairs hold contests to settle whose is best. One pub, the George Inn at Frant, hosted one called the World Sloe Gin Championships, and in 2016 the judges, tasting blind, gave all of the top six places to sloe gins made at home. One maker, who reports winning it twice, wrote of trying the way fruit liqueurs are made in Croatia: leaving the jars in the sun.

That's my favourite part. A blind tasting can't ask who you got your recipe from. It can only ask whether it's good. I like to think every home-made gin on that table began as somebody else's and ended up as its maker's own. That's what you do with what you were given: every name attached, every piece tried, and only what survived handed over.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Blackthorn, a classic that a barman in London was already calling very old in 1922, when it came two different ways. Of the five a 1947 bar guide printed, I kept the one built from gin, sloe gin and dry vermouth, with orange bitters, because the sloe gin is already sweetened and the dry vermouth lets the fruit show. It's stirred until very cold, served small with no ice. At the end, a lemon peel gets one pinch over the glass, for the scent. Use a traditional sloe gin, bought or made by someone you know, and keep one rule: the two gins always make 60 ml between them. Taste the sloe gin first. The sweeter it is, the less of it and the more of the plain gin. I left that call to you as a nod to those pub contests: whatever the recipe says, your own taste decides.

You're afraid it ends with you. It doesn't. Somewhere, someone already starts a sentence with your name, and you just haven't been there to hear it. So don't wait for someone to ask, or until you're old. This year, teach one thing you were taught to someone who'll keep it, and tell them the bit you changed, and why. That's how you end up among the people you quote.
